utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case Number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you to the registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I'm turning to the Defence now. Could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, main counsel, and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On this day, I would like to welcome everyone, the 17th of May, 215th day of the trial. I would just like to welcome everyone present here, General Hadzihasanovic and General Kubura. And I would also like to welcome the registrar, the legal assistants, the usher, and the entire staff assisting us in our work, both in and outside the courtroom. Last week we had no hearings and so we shall continue with our work now by hearing of a witness which had been planned. But before we do that, there are a number of points outstanding. I'm going to ask General Kubura's Defence team to explain the state of affairs, that is to say apparently they intend to withdraw certain witnesses and to call certain witnesses on the basis of the Rule 92 bis and to tender certain documents with regard to Rules -- again, with regard to the Rule, 92 bis. Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I could take this opportunity as Your Honours have requested to outline what the state of affairs is now for the defence for Mr. Kubura. There is a witness, as Your Honours know, to be called today live. That is witness number 8 on our list, and that will be the last live witness to be called by the Defence for Mr. Kubura. We'll have no further witnesses after that, but for two 92 bis statements which are currently being prepared. And those are for witness number 5 on the list and witness number 9. I could mention the names, if we were to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could we go into private session, then.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have two other points to deal with in the open session. The first one has to do with the Defence documents with regard to which no decision has been taken as yet because we were in the process of putting all this together and finding out what was still missing in terms of translations, either in English or in B/C/S. Finally, I'm in a position to tell you that almost all documents have been translated now and it appears that we only have one document, number 400, to be dealt with. And there again, on Thursday we'll be able to submit a decision in writing or at the very least an oral decision. Because apart from this document, almost everything else has been dealt with. That's the first point. And the second point, we are still pondering the Prosecution's motion with regard to the re-opening of this burden of proof with regard -- of the case with regard to the admission of 24 documents. In the meantime we have heard over the past few days that the Prosecution would reserve the right to give an oral presentation of their position following the Defence's submissions, and we also gather that General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team wanted to submit an additional motion orally with regard to this same matter. So the best thing to do would be since we shall have some time to deal with this on Thursday, it would be a good idea if the Defence through Mr. Bourgon could make those additional comments. And then I will be giving the floor to the other Defence team for General Kubura, if necessary, and then the Prosecution, and they will again make an oral presentation of their own point of view. Mr. Bourgon, is my understanding of the situation correct? Is this indeed correct, the fact that you want to make some additional comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I would just like to specify that these are not additional comments or anything, but documents that we would like to add. They will be enclosed to our case. It is a letter that we have received from the Government of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this document would show that certain documents that the Prosecution is seeking to tender had already been in their possession two years ago. And so apparently they had received those documents in the course of 2002. Obviously we're not in a position to say whether the information that we received from the government is exact. All we want is to tender this letter and that's all we want to do in order to be able to continue along the same lines. I have the document here with me. If you wish me to do so, I could submit it to you today or maybe wait until Thursday. Whichever you prefer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, have you shown this document to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, yes, has been faxed to the Prosecution and so they will have received a copy and we discussed this a bit earlier. And my learned friend suggested that it might be preferable to discuss that on Thursday. We are open to any suggestions. The only thing is you should tell us whether you would like to see the document today or wait until Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right then. If my understanding of the situation is correct, it is a letter that you received after your submissions and it came from the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And it reveals, apparently, that the Prosecution has had these documents, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. certain documents, in their possession for a number of years. And now you have this letter which has been sent to you very recently and you would simply like to add this letter to your submissions. Am I correct, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite correct, Mr. President. And this is the reason why we asked to delay our response, in fact, because we had been informed that we would be getting this letter on Friday rather late, and we thought that we could submit it together with a motion on Monday. Unfortunately, it was not possible because we only received the letter on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Mr. Mundis, you have heard what Mr. Bourgon has just told us. Now, this official document coming from the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina is already in your possession, which is going to allow you on Thursday to respond in general terms to all these points. First of all, the Defence's submissions and the document itself. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. My learned colleague, Mr. Bourgon, is in fact correct. We did receive the letter he has spoken about. He has faxed that to us late last week. It does appear to be the case, Mr. President, that nine of the proposed exhibits attached to the Prosecution's application for re-opening were or have been in the possession of the Office of the Prosecution since October 2002. We are currently in the process of determining precisely what happened to this material, and that is one of the reasons why I discussed this matter with the Chamber's Legal Officer and suggested that perhaps Thursday would be the best opportunity for us to be fully informed, to the extent that's possible, and to convey the requisite information to the Trial Chamber. At this point, let me simply indicate that the documents in question, Mr. President, are those which are identified in our application to re-open as coming from the Bosnian intelligence service, that is the OSA documents, there are nine of them that were attached to our application. They are easily recognisable by the solid black border on the documents, and it is that material which is Prosecution received both in October 2002 and then again in October 2004. There has previously been some discussions about the electronic format in which those documents were made available to the Prosecution, and I will again be in a position to further discuss this matter with the Trial Chamber on Thursday. I do anticipate that we will be in a position to fully articulate our position with respect to these nine documents. At this point in time, I simply felt that it was important for the Trial Chamber to be aware of this fact because of our previous position that we were not relying on any documents that were in our possession prior to the closing of the Prosecution case. And in fact, these nine documents were received by a Defence investigator in October 2002 on a CD, but once they were delivered to the -- excuse me to a Prosecution investigator. I said "Defence investigator." So an investigator of the OTP in October 2002, they were submitted to the evidence unit, and at that point in time, Mr. President, we are still undertaking some queries to determine what exactly happened to that material once it went into the evidence unit. I would be grateful for an opportunity to further elaborate upon this on Thursday once I am in a better position to inform the Chamber as to what precisely happened. And again, as Your Honour noted, we are still awaiting the translation of the response to our application from the Hadzihasanovic Defence team. I expect that translation sometime later today. We may seek leave to reply to that, but I would be prepared, Mr. President, in order to expedite the proceedings to respond -- or to -- if the Chamber permits me to reply, to do so orally on Thursday as well so that we can in effect wrap up all of the various parties' legal submissions concerning the application to re-open on Thursday, and that would be the course that we would propose be undertaken, so as to move this matter to its conclusion as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, as you might suspect, we have spent a great many hours contemplating this issue. Since we need a decision, you will have a decision either in writing or orally on Thursday. You've just confirmed the fact -- the following fact, that is to say that nine documents coming from the OTP -- OSA were in your possession since October 2002. It's on page 11 and 17 -- line 17 of the transcript. And just from memory I can say that I remember that in the letter that was addressed to -- obviously it was indicated that you had 796 exhibits and 114 electronic-format documents. And I'm wondering whether this is correct, because it was not indicated in the initial letter and in your submissions you made no reference to that. So I said to myself, "What does this figure of 114 correspond to?" And now it appears that amongst those 114 there are these famous nine documents. Now, on Thursday you will be telling us what extra information you have, but can you confirm as of now that these nine documents were indeed in your possession since October 2002, perhaps not yours personally but that the Prosecution as such had received that information on a CD.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution will confirm that in October 2002 a CD was delivered to the field office in Sarajevo and was subsequently brought here to The Hague. The investigator who received that CD entered that CD into the evidence unit. I am not in a position at this point in time to confirm what, if anything, was done with that CD until over the weekend, following receipt of the facts from Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Neuner and another member of the OTP staff retrieved that CD from the evidence unit on Friday and began reviewing the material that was contained on that CD. I am not in a position to confirm -- other than the fact that this CD was received and placed in the evidence unit, I am not in a position to inform the Trial Chamber as to any steps taken by anyone within the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to the material that was contained on that CD. And that, Mr. President, is precisely the questions I am seeking to have answered so that I can inform the Trial Chamber what steps, if any, were taken with respect to viewing the material that was contained on that CD. I will confirm, however, that a CD with 114 electronic files on it and a number, apparently, of subfiles, if you will, was in fact received by the Office of the Prosecutor in October 2002. What was done with that CD, other than the fact that it was submitted to the evidence unit until just a few days ago, I am not in a position because we are attempting to determine the answers to that question. And as the Trial Chamber might appreciate, virtually all of the staff members who have worked on this case are -- there are only a few people left from the investigation phase of this case. So it means attempting to locate former staff members who are no longer with this institution and who are working in various places around the world, and so communications with some of them has been not as easy as we would have liked. So we're trying to find the answers to these very questions, but to make -- to be right to the point, Mr. President, we have had this material in the evidence unit since October of 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis, for this information. We'll see things more clearly on Thursday because by Thursday you should have had sufficient time to look into the matter. You will then confirm whether or not you in fact had these nine documents. Is there anything you would like to add, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Not on this point, Mr. President, but I would simply -- perhaps it was simply an oversight, but with respect to the Kubura 92 bis statements and documents, I believe, for the record it would be important to have the Hadzihasanovic position stated with respect to that material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll give the floor to General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team. What is your position with regard to the three documents that concern the two 92 bis witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we agree with what you have suggested and with Brigadier Kubura's Defence team, we have no objections to make to the comments made by our colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Bourgon again, who is on his feet already, I would like to point out that the Chamber believes that on Thursday the Prosecution will provide an oral answer to all the issues raised. That involves a response to the Defence submissions, and the Prosecution should also inform us of its position with regard to the famous letter from the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities, which was disclosed by the Defence to the Prosecution over the weekend. This should enable us to save time and by Thursday we should already be informed of the Prosecution's position with regard to all these issues and with regard to the motion to re-open its case. The Chamber will, naturally, gladly accept this letter being communicated to the -- communicated through the Legal Officer through Mr. Bourgon, I'm referring to the letter from the Bosnia and Herzegovina authorities. This should enable us to save time. Mr. Bourgon, I will give the floor to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is what I wanted to raise. I have the letter with me -- this is the issue I wanted to raise. I can provide you with the letter immediately. I have the original letter in B/C/S and I have a translation from the CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The usher will collect the letter and copies will be made of the letter. We'll now go back into open session. Madam Registrar, let's go back into open session -- in fact, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are already in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are. We are in fact in open session. Before we call the witness into the courtroom, I would just like to point out that the Legal Officer informed you of a provisional schedule which should make it possible for the case to be closed by mid-July. Initially we will have submissions, written submissions, from both parties, and then there will be the closing arguments. As far as the first stage is concerned, since the Prosecution works in English, it would be good if the Defence's submissions were also drafted in English. This should allow the Prosecution, when it takes the floor, to present its arguments because if they have their submissions in English they will be able to present their arguments. For -- if they have to wait for an English translation, this might be problematic. This concerns General Hadzihasanovic's Defence above all. Would that be a problem for you to have your submissions in English, although you are very good in French, too?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I must admit I'm a little surprise by the Chamber's request. We can write in English or in French; that is not a problem if the Chamber so desires. We can write our written submission in English. If we do -- if we write our submissions in French, this is not to cause any problems, but it's only to enable the Chamber to have the document in French. But if the Chamber would like our final brief to be in English, well, we will draft it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that Mr. Mundis would appreciate that. That will enable him to prepare. Is there anything else that has to be addressed, any other technical issues that have to be addressed by either of the parties before we call the witness into the courtroom? If not, I will ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving interpretation of what I'm saying. If so, please say you can hear and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for General Kubura's Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, could you tell me your first and last names, your date of birth, and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Osman Hasanagic. I was born in Rogatica in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 16th of September, 1957. I live in Sarajevo and I work in the Klas company as the chief of the legal department, the head of the legal department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993, what was your occupation? And if you were a member of the military, which unit were you a member of and what rank did you hold or what position did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 at the beginning of the war, I was in Rogatica in my place of birth. The first job I had was in the administration of social revenue as an inspector. And then later I went to the Klas Sarajevo company and became a manager of the bakery, which was part of the Klas company in Sarajevo. When the war broke out, I was in Rogatica with my family and I remained there until the 19th of June of the same year, when the Serbian enemy committed a total act of aggression against the population of Bosnia. On that day, the entire Bosniak population that had remained in Rogatica was either expelled or killed. Panic spread.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could you tell me which unit you were assigned to then, where you were then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in Rogatica. I was among the population and I worked until the 15th of May, 1992. And then a real blockade developed. It wasn't possible to leave, and the people naturally remained in Rogatica and some of them fled in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but were you assigned to a combat unit of any kind? And if so, which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time there were no organised units. We were all in a certain sense members of the Territorial Defence from the 8th of April, 1992, but this wasn't adequately organised. And it didn't have the characteristics of a defence system. The people were not armed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But later, which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Rogatica fell on the 19th of June, 1992, my family and I and the other inhabitants went over the mountains towards Sarajevo. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are providing too lengthy responses. I want to know which unit you were assigned to. We know you were a member of the Territorial Defence, but then which unit were you assigned to? Let's leave your family aside and let's deal with the military unit you were assigned to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I went to Gorazde and I joined the Territorial Defence there, or rather the Rogatica Brigade that had been established. I was a private in that unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The end of 1992, on the 24th of December to be more precise, with permission from the command of the brigade, from Gorazde, I went to the free territory with my family. I intended to go to Sarajevo. However, since Sarajevo was under a total blockade, it was only possible to go to Zenica where I had some friends and some relatives of my wife's. This trip took us seven days and on the 1st of January --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that your trip lasted for seven days is very interesting, but that tells me nothing about the unit you were assigned to. Which unit were you assigned to in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I arrived in Zenica, I reported to the Territorial Defence Staff in order to be put on the record, and I wanted to continue working in the army. I was told that there was no position for me there at the time, but I was told to try with the 314th Brigade, to try and report to the 314th Brigade or to the 7th Muslim Brigade. I first went to the 314th Brigade, however the lowest position had been taken so I then went to the 7th Muslim Brigade where I knew Mr. Halil Brzina, as we had played handball together. He was the assistant commander for logistics. I knew him because of his interest in handball. This happened at the beginning of July 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So we found out that you joined the 7th Muslim Brigade. Could you tell me whether you have already testified before an international or a national court about the events that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are a lawyer, it will be very easy for you to understand the information I am now going to provide you with. I would like to inform you of the procedure that we will be following today. If everything runs smoothly, it won't be necessary for you to return tomorrow. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by Brigadier Kubura's Defence counsel, and you will certainly met his counsel in the course of your proofing. Once you have answered the questions put to you, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct what is called their cross-examination. Once this stage has been completed, Brigadier Kubura's Defence team can ask you additional questions that relate to the responses you have given to the Prosecution in the course of their cross-examination. As far as General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team is concerned, once the examination-in-chief has been completed they may also put questions to you. The three Judges, who are sitting before you, may also ask you questions, but as a rule the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to complete their examination before intervening. Very often -- as very often, the questions that the Judges want to ask a witness will have already been asked by one of the parties. It's not necessary to intervene unnecessarily; this is why we prefer to wait for the parties to complete their examination and cross-examination before we put questions to witnesses. If we put questions to you, we will do so for two reasons. Firstly, we may ask you questions because we believe that the answers you have provided to the parties require clarification or because given the position you held or the positions you held in various units, we believe that there's certain information that might assist the Judges. And we will then ask you questions to obtain this information. Once the Judges have put their questions to you, we will then give the floor to both parties again, and the Defence will be the last to take the floor to put any questions to you that they believe might be of interest to them. There are two other issues I would like to draw your attention to. You have taken the solemn declaration, which as a lawyer you should know excludes the possibility of giving false testimony. False testimony is punishable. And there is also something very specific to our procedure; it is somewhat complicated. I would like to point out that the witness may refuse to answer a question if the witness believes that his answer might subsequently be used against him to -- if the witness believes that this might incriminate him. But in such a case -- this has never arisen to date, but in such a case the Chamber may give the witness a form of immunity but compel the witness to answer the question. In such a position, the procedure followed is an oral procedure. This is why you will see that everything you say is interpreted and appears on the screen that is in front of you. This is why the answers you provide are so important. Try to answer the questions extensively, but avoid going off on a tangent. Try to answer the questions put to you precisely. If you fail to understand a question, don't hesitate to ask the party putting the question to you to rephrase the question. In the course of the proceedings, the parties might show you military documents to ask you whether you can recognise the documents. The Defence or the Prosecution might show you such documents, and sometimes in exceptional cases the Judges might show you such documents, too. If you run into any difficulties in the course of the proceedings, do inform us of the fact. In about three-quarters of an hour we will be having a break, and there will be a second break, too. The purpose of the break is to allow you to have a rest, since answering questions incessantly can be tiring, and secondly it's necessary for the technicians to change the tapes. This is how we will be proceeding, and without wasting anymore time, I will now give the floor to the Defence for their examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Presiding Judge you said where you were in 1992 and 1993. I will first ask you, you said that in 1992 you were in Rogatica when the war broke out. Where is Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Rogatica is 68 kilometres from Sarajevo. It's in Eastern Bosnia. There were about 8.000 inhabitants in the town, and there were about 24.000 inhabitants in the municipality. As far as the Bosniak and Serbian population is concerned, the ratio was 64 to 36 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in June 1992 you were in Rogatica and that you then went to Gorazde. Can you tell us where Gorazde is located?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Gorazde is 30 kilometres by motorway from Rogatica, but given the blockade of the roads from May 1992 onwards, it wasn't possible to use that road. When Rogatica fell on the 19th of June, 1992, the people had to use mountain paths, so-called goat paths. And they'd use these mountainous paths when we left at 2.00 in the morning and went to the first village, and when we arrived in the village of Ragole [phoen] -- Well, this trip lasted for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Where is Gorazde? In which part of Bosnia and Herzegovina is it located in?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Gorazde is in Eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in December 1992 you and your family left Gorazde. Who were your family members? Who did you leave Gorazde with?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: My -- there were four members of my core family, my wife, myself, and my children. My daughter, Jasna, 4 years old, and my son Zlatko 6-years-old. We went over Grebak a well-known mountain. There was over a metre of snow. We had no food. We had no money. We had nothing. Our only chance was to try and reach the free territory, and I received permission to do so from the then-commander Mr. Burbasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you arrived in Zenica. How long did your journey last and how did you go there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: That journey lasted seven days. We went there on foot all the way there, mostly at night because we were afraid that we would be intercepted. We feared what might happen to us. We went over Mountain Igman. We were on Mountain Igman for two days, and then over Trnovo, too. We spent two days at Trnovo, too. We went over Tarcin we spent one day going over Tarcin, and on the seventh day we reached Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive in Zenica exactly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: We arrived in Zenica on the 1st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that it took you seven days and seven nights to get there. What's the distance between Gorazde and Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the exact distance is, given the roads, given the paths we took, the mountains and certain secondary routes, it's difficult to say. But I'm quite sure that it was about 300 or 400 kilometres if you go there by such a route.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: You said that upon your arrival at Zenica you reported to the Territorial Defence. You don't need to repeat all that, but I'm interested to find out when exactly you arrived at the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I got to the 7th Muslim Brigade on the 7th of July, 1993. I went for an interview at the brigade command, and I was received first and foremost by Mr. Halil Brzina, whom I had known before the war because we played handball together. And so we were both athletes together. He explained to me that he needed a legal officer, and he introduced me to Mr. Amir Kubura, who was the Chief of Staff and who also welcomed me very nicely and wished me straight away to be able to join the 7th Muslim Brigade. He explained to me the basic principles and what my duties would be. And thereupon I accepted immediately to join the 7th Muslim Brigade, where I was told that there was a vacancy for a duty legal officer there and there had been a vacancy for a long time. Basically the name of the post was the officer for legal affairs of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: My next question was going to be exactly that, what was your position within the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I've just told you that I was the officer for legal affairs of the 7th Muslim Brigade and I was directly accountable to the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know who the commander was at that time when you joined the 7th Muslim Brigade I mean?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: At that time I did not know what was the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade, but my first interview, or rather my second interview was with Mr. Amir Kubura, who was the Chief of Staff. At that time I had no knowledge as to who the commander of the brigade was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever get to find out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: A short time later I found out that the brigade commander was Mr. Asim Koricic and that he had actually been absent for a long time already, that he was on an official leave. And I made no further inquiries as to his whereabouts and why he was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your office, since you were a legal officer of the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I was in a small office which is situated at the command office building. And I was the only legal officer at the time. And next to us there was another building for another battalion, and then there was another part of the building where there was a restaurant and an entrance to the Bilmiste hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: That was in the same building where your office was. And were there any offices for the other members of the command there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that building there was the office for the brigade commander, the deputy commander, the Chief of Staff. My own office was there and -- and a part of another command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where Mr. Kubura's office was?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kubura's office was across the hall from the office of the commander of the brigade, and it said at the door of his office "Chief of Staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Until when did you remain in that position as a legal officer for the 7th Brigade, or were there any changes of your status or any change of your duties later on?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: The duties of the legal affairs officer was something that I carried out between the 7th of July, 1993, and the month of April 1994, when I was appointed as assistant commander for legal affairs -- or rather, the department was called legal affairs sector or department. And I was given the rank of captain, and I -- and it was on the basis of the orders of our command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are going to be using two documents only with this witness. So if you agree, we could first of all show the document from 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanagic, could you take a look at the document number 2192 dated the 11th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, Mr. President, it's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to take a look at it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: It reflects what you have told us about about your duties when you joined the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Hasanagic, can you tell the Court about when you joined the 7th Muslim Brigade. What was the situation, taking into account your own job, rules, regulations, et cetera, what was your job in fact?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: When I joined the 7th Muslim Brigade, I found a state of affairs which was rather unsettled and confused with regard to rules and regulations. I was not provided with any documentation, any set of rules, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. laws, regulations, any legal publications, official journals, or anything that would provide a basis for my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: When you joined the 7th Muslim Brigade, did you ask for assistance or suggestions as to how you could do your job?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I did ask for assistance and I did get it from the command of the 3rd Corps, the department for legal affairs, especially from Mr. Jusuf Halilagic who was assistant commander for legal affairs of the 3rd Corps, who introduced me to my job and my duties, and he provided me with indispensable assistance and he gave me some documents, some rules and regulations, and he clarified a little bit what they normally did at the corps and what I was supposed to do at the 7th Muslim Brigade. And I can say that I got all the assistance from Mr. Halilagic, who, as I say, introduced me to my job and the way in which I was supposed to carry out my duties. And thereupon, I had a somewhat clearer picture as to what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next question, I would like to ask you the following: Prior to that had you ever worked at any courts within the judicial system at all or any other system having to do with judicial matters?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. Up until that time -- as I said, my first job was as inspector for financial matters and was not in business. And afterwards I moved into the business world. And so I had no connection, nothing to do with the judicial matters in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: What were your duties as a legal affairs officer?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: My duties and obligations were to apply the rules of the military service very rigorously as well as the laws and to provide full expert support to the command of the brigade and the subordinate units in terms of implementing rules, laws, and regulations, which regulated the way they should behave in war and which regulated warfare in general. My second duty was to provide legal assistance to all members of the brigade with regard to any urgent status matters, considering the fact that the overwhelming majority of those fighters were refugees and had no proper housing and were almost starving. They would get one aid package a month. So I spent a great deal of my time dealing with the civilian authorities, with a view of solving those urgent matters pertaining to housing. And in quite a few cases, I was successful. Obviously the brigade had its own criteria, its own lists of priorities such as, for example, the families of soldiers who had either died or been wounded, then wounded soldiers, and then -- only then healthy and fit members of the armed forces. Also, my other duties included the implementation and application of rules and regulations, especially with regard to criminal proceedings, and the -- point 16 of the Criminal Code -- Penal Code of the former Yugoslavia which had -- which was still in force on the basis of a decree, and that referred to any crimes against humanity such as genocide, any crimes committed against civilians or prisoners of war or the sick and wounded. Obviously in that part of my job, it was my duty to apply the rules and to thus instruct and set an example for the brigade and the subordinated units in order to make sure that all soldiers were well-acquainted with those rules and that they would indeed apply those rules in the field, or rather in the course of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. You can finish.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Throughout that period, I had a great deal of assistance and support from Mr. Amir Kubura, who throughout that period insisted that all the rules and regulations and all the legal provisions should be applied strictly. And he made sure that he applied them rigorously. Of course he was in a position to do that because of his authority and his -- and the fact this he was very familiar with the military doctrine. Apart from that, within the 7th Muslim Brigade there was a service called military security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for interrupting you. You can come back to that later. But when you mentioned instructing, educating, soldiers, could you clarify that? What did you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: What I meant was that Mr. Amir Kubura asked me to give lectures to members of our units and to alert them and engage in preventative action with regard to the behaviour which is appropriate in war and to warn them of sanctions in case any crimes were committed, any crimes in -- which would represent an infringement of the Geneva Convention with regard to the civilian population, the wounded, medical staff, and also property, the property that belonged to third parties. Apart from that, it was also my task to react in case any infringements were reported by the security services with regard to disciplinary measures. Any investigations were conducted by the security service. And once we got reports of these infringements of the rules of behaviour, which would indicate that disciplinary proceedings were called for, I would get a statement from the accused and gather evidence and qualify the infringements in question and try and determine how serious it was. And then I would draft a possible decision, a proposed decision, for a penalty and for the measures that were called for - measures or punishments, depending on how serious the infringement was - and such a decision in the form of a proposal would then be submitted to Mr. Amir Kubura. For the most part, Mr. Amir Kubura would go along with my suggestions and would sign these draft documents as to the disciplinary measures to be imposed upon members of the brigade. Normally those were not very serious crimes, and most penalties were up to seven days in detention or maximum was 30 or 60 days in detention for more serious infringements.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you here. Do you know when Mr. Kubura became commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kubura became commander by the beginning of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you mentioned these disciplinary procedures or infringements, could you clarify a little bit. What sorts of infringements were we talking about? What sorts of offences? What did they refer to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: All those infringements were described in the set of rules and regulations with regard to disciplinary accountability. And for the most part, we were talking about people leaving the unit of their own accord or damaging the reputation of the unit by maybe petty thefts of ammunition and MTS for disturbing others or not obeying the orders of their superiors, and a whole range of other matters such as disturbing public law and order and what have you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Where would those penalties be imposed and how would people be detained?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: People were detained at the premises of our own brigade up to seven days. And everything in excess of seven days would mean that the person in question would be sent to the correction institution at Zenica, and they would be escorted there by our own security officers. We recorded all the comings and goings, and thereupon the detainee would be brought back to the unit to resume his duties. As to penalties of more than 30 days in prison, more serious penalties, were also imposed at this penal and correctional facility at Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, perhaps we could move on to a another topic now, but maybe this is the right time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we will have a technical break now and we shall come back at around 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: --- Upon resuming at 4.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume and I'll give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanagic, in the department that you worked in as a legal officer, were you alone or were there any other individuals who worked there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, I worked alone. There was no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before the break you mentioned the security service. I interrupted you at that point. You mentioned the 7th Brigade security service. Among the duties you had to perform as a legal officer, did you get involved at all with the work of the security service?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: The security service acted independently. It was organised as a military security service. It had its assistant commander, its officers, and military policemen. They worked according to their own rules and regulations. They had rules and regulations concerning military security. Their field of work was governed by those rules. I did not have much contact with them. Our work did not overlap, apart from when they would ask for certain rules or laws to be interpreted. And they would also ask for me to provide them with certain instructions or assist them professionally with some of their work. I had no other contact with them, apart from the fact that I already mentioned that I worked in accordance with their reports when it came to instituting criminal proceedings [as interpreted] against members of our unit for offences that I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a legal officer, was it possible for you to participate in investigations or to conduct investigations?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, that was not my duty. That was -- that fell within the field of competence of the security service. They alone were responsible for such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the assistant commander for security was? Who was in charge of the security service?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: The assistant commander for security was Mr. Nesib Talic. I know him by profession. He had his offices, his security service, or rather his military policemen. He was directly accountable to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, Mr. President, on page 33, line 19 it should say "disciplinary measures," not "criminal proceedings."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you exchange correspondence with the security service at all?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, in that I had to respond to the reports they would file, and I would have to continue working on the proceedings instituted. I had to draft decisions on disciplinary responsibility and forward them to the brigade commander as a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think this is in the transcript. What do you say Mr. Talic was by profession?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Talic was a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a legal officer, did you participate in taking decisions drafting orders on bringing people in?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at the second document that is before you, and perhaps you could comment on the document. I showed you this document in the course of the proofing.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I've managed to read through this order. It's been signed by the assistant commander for security, Mr. Nesib Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out item 2 in the order. It's an order dated September 1993.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: "It shall be prohibited to arrest or apprehend persons without approval from the assistant commander for security or from persons he has authorised."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could you read out item 1.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: "Searching flats and other closed premises by military policemen without approval from the assistant commander for security or from persons whom he has authorised to issue such approval is hereby prohibited."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Before I showed you this document, I asked you whether as a legal officer you were in a position to take part in drafting such orders? Were you familiar with such orders?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. I would never receive such orders nor was I involved in the drafting of such orders. The assistant commander followed the rules of service for the military security service when he was involved in his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did the security service cooperate with the 3rd Corps security service?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The security service cooperated closely with the military security service of the 3rd Corps, or rather of the Military Police Battalion. They carried out orders. They forwarded orders to the higher command and acted in accordance with orders. It was their duty to act in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Given your answer, I will now ask you who was responsible for conducting investigations in the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: The military security service alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hasanagic, do you know where the music school is located?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The music school is about 2 kilometres from the 7th Muslim Brigade command, or rather it was located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who stayed in the music school, who was responsible for the music school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: The military security service was responsible for the music school, and there was a military detention unit there. And after I arrived for a brief period of time there was a military clinic for the wounded from the 7th Muslim Brigade that was located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the music school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I never had the opportunity of visiting the music school, nor did I have the opportunity of seeing the military detention unit there. I went there, I went to the clinic at a later date to visit a soldier, and there is nothing else that I can tell you about the music school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: As a legal officer in the brigade, did you have the opportunity of attending meetings of the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: As the legal officer, quite rarely. But when I did attend such meetings, they never discussed the music school. Later when I became the assistant commander for legal affairs, I regularly attended meetings and briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Talic ever raise any issues that related to the music school and what happened in the music school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Never in my presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did he ask questions at the meetings that you attended in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, he didn't, especially not when he was no longer a member of the military security service. I'm talking about the period when I became Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the assistant commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about the conditions in the music school, under what sort of conditions people were taken there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I acted on requests to institute disciplinary proceedings, and this only concerned members of our brigade. As far as other individuals were concerned, I wouldn't receive any reports or any information. I wouldn't receive documents of any kind that had to do with other individuals who might have been detained in that detention unit. If I had had any such documents, I would have acted on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever take a statement from anyone who was not a member of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, never. Only from members of the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, do you know up until when Mr. Kubura was in the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Amir Kubura was the commander of the brigade until April 1994. I personally attended a meeting of the command when he was informed of the transfer to other duties. No other explanation was provided. I was personally quite surprised by this decision and by this explanation because my personal and professional position was that I should comply with all the orders, all the documents, issued by the brigade commander. I think that he was an exceptional officer. He had a lot of authority. He was impartial, and he would not spare himself nor would he spare others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no further questions. This completes our examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now give the floor to General Hadzihasanovic's Defence team, if they have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hasanagic, my name is Edina Residovic and together with my colleague, Stephane Bourgon, I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic. When answering the questions put to you by my learned friend you said that on the 7th of July you arrived in the 7th Muslim Brigade and you were then appointed as the legal officer there. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Up until that point in time, the legal matters that you have referred to were not dealt with by lawyers. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a lawyer who arrived in Zenica as a refugee, could you confirm that at that time there were a lot of -- there was a great demand for lawyers in the army, but it wasn't possible to satisfy all these demands because some lawyers had left Zenica and many others were working for the judiciary. So it was not at all surprising that up until that point in time, the 7th Muslim Brigade did not have a lawyer. Is that the situation you came across in the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would be, roughly speaking, the situation that I encountered. There wasn't a sufficient amount of -- sufficient number of lawyers, social workers, doctors.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Not only in our unit, but in other units, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you describe your duties you said that you spent a lot of time on social issues that concerned the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. My question is as follows: Since, as can be seen from the evidence presented here to date, it's quite clear that the 7th Muslim Brigade was composed of quite a large number of refugees, and the problem you came across was significant. People did not have premises where they could stay and live with their families. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I believe that that is one of the most significant problems, the social status of the refugees. And I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, would you agree with me, Mr. Hasanagic, if I said that that problem could not be dealt with by the 7th Muslim Brigade or by any other brigade or corps because when it came to distributing abandoned property, flats, socially owned flats or privately owned flats, when it came to distributing such property, only the competent authorities in Zenica could deal with such matters?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct. There were no military flats that could be allocated by the army. And as far as all the abandoned flats are concerned, the municipal service, or rather the municipal secretariat for residential issues was responsible for this. They would keep records on flats that have been abandoned and the command would contact them in order to try and resolve the housing problems that their members had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My following question is as follows. You said that in the brigade you would establish a list of people who had priorities. Your criteria for priorities involved suggesting to the authorities that they take into account the priorities that you had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you assumed your position as legal officer, you said that you were greatly assisted by the 3rd Corps command and in particular by Mr. Halilagic who was the head of the legal department in the 3rd Corps. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is the best form of assistance that I received. Without their assistance, I couldn't have performed my duties in an adequate manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hasanagic, would you agree with me if I said that by cooperating with the 3rd Corps and Mr. Halilagic, it was possible for you to see that the 3rd Corps took respect for discipline in the army very seriously?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. The 3rd Corps issued binding orders for all brigades, and that included the 7th Muslim Brigade, too. They issued orders stating that all the rules and laws of war should be abided by.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that's my following question. You said that you received from Mr. Halilagic various documents and instructions. Would it be correct to say that among the instructions that you received there were instructions and copies of the Criminal Code of the SFRY, and this assisted you in the brigades when it came to explaining the duties and obligations that the soldiers had?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Halilagic provided me with his own copy of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you whether when performing your duties you were able to determine if the 3rd Corps position was that it was necessary to train not just members of the command but the soldiers in the brigades so that they could understand and respect orders and abide by the law. Is this something that you observed when trying to implement the policies of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received such instructions and we behaved in accordance with the instructions. Whenever it was possible in our free time we would inform everyone of these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you answered a question and said that you were also involved in providing instruction, this is part of your duties, when it comes to abiding by the rules and by the laws, was this part of the instructions and the training that you provided for units that were subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the legal basis for interpreting the orders, for implementing them. This is how instruction was provided in order to ensure that all army members were discouraged from committing illegal acts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also asked a question from my colleague, Mr. Ibrisimovic, about instituting disciplinary proceedings for offences or misdemeanours. Tell me, was it the 3rd Corps policy that anyone who had committed an offence, a misdemeanour, had to be held accountable?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the position of the 3rd Corps command and of the command of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When preparing professional documents for the brigade commander, initially the Chief of Staff, as you said, and then the brigade commander, you adhered to such -- to those instructions very strictly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, and all my proposals and instructions were respected by the brigade commander, Mr. Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And there were no members of your brigade who would be exempt from responsibility if it was established that he had committed some sort of an offence?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: There were no exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were involved in instituting proceedings, both members of the brigade and battalion commanders. There were measures taken at all levels if you determined that an offence or crime had been committed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Everyone was treated in the same way, regardless of whether they were officers or just privates.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Hasanagic, before you arrived there, the duties you tried to perform consistently and to the best of your ability were performed as best as possible by members of the brigade command, to the extent they were capable of doing that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, to the extent they were capable of performing these duties, that was done and I think that we were capable of performing those duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm now going to give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is -- my name is Daryl Mundis and along with my colleagues represent the Prosecution in this case. I do have a few questions for you, sir, but before starting I want to reassure you that it is not our intention in any way to confuse you and I would ask you that in the event you don't understand one of my questions, please simply say so and I will rephrase the question so that you do understand it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me start out, sir, by asking you to clarify, if you can, the relationship between yourself, as the 7th Muslim Brigade legal officer, and the district military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I very rarely had any opportunity to get in touch with them directly. On a couple of occasions, I visited the district prosecution offices and the court for some points of interpretation, in order to offer legal assistance when members of the 7th Muslim Brigade were accused of some misdemeanours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, approximately how many times from the 7th of July, 1993, until the end of 1993 you had the opportunity to have interaction with judges or prosecutors or investigating judges of the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Three to four times, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you, sir, at any point in time from 7 July 1993 through the end of 1993 have any dealings with the district military court in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain to us a little bit more about the role that you had, again focussing on the period in 1993 when you were the legal officer, your role with respect to any cases that were sent to the district military court in Zenica for further investigation and possible Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the witness has already answered, but my objection is that the witness has already said that he had never been involved in any investigations. So perhaps we could clarify the question in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that you personally were not involved in any investigations and that the 7th Muslim Brigade security service was responsible for investigations. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In the event Mr. Talic, the assistant commander for security, or any of his security service personnel wanted to submit a case to the district military court in Zenica for further investigation or perhaps Prosecution, would you have been involved in any way in terms of reviewing that material or providing advice or did you get a copy of such material that was submitted to the military court? Can you tell us a little bit about your role as the legal officer in that process with the security service in the district military court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Talic, that is to say the security service, never submitted to me any written documents and they never asked me for any assistance when it was a matter of dealing with any crimes. The security services worked within the framework of their duties and what they were authorised to do. And they had close cooperation with the security service of the 3rd Corps. I'm not aware of any cases and I'm certain of that. I'm not aware of any document of such nature coming from Mr. Talic having been addressed to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, if you were aware - and I'm not, again, in any way suggesting that you were personally involved in any investigations - but were you aware in your capacity as a legal officer of any member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade being investigated, charged, disciplined, or in any other way prosecuted for alleged crimes committed in the Zenica music school in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I never received any such information and any such information was never available to me. Had I had that, I would have known what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware at any point in time, sir, from the -- from your appointment as legal officer to the end of 1993 about rumours concerning mistreatment of persons being detained in the Zenica music school?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. I knew of no rumours because it was not a part of my job description, and I had not heard any rumours about anyone whatsoever having been mistreated in any way. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, or did you in any way come across any documents or information concerning any member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade who was investigated, charged, disciplined, or in any way prosecuted with respect to alleged crimes that occurred in Vares in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. Not a single document of that nature ever reached me and I have no knowledge of any proceedings having been brought against anyone with regard to Vares.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time, sir, upon your arrival at the 7th Muslim Brigade in early July 1993, were there any records or documents pertaining to legal matters or case files that you in any way reviewed with respect to cases that had been conducted prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. Upon my arrival, I found not a single scrap of paper or any information or any documents, nothing, in as far as the legal matters are concerned. And as to the documentation of the military security services, I had no access to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us a few moments ago, sir, about the few occasions that you had interactions with the district military court in Zenica. Do you recall the specifics of any of the cases involving soldiers of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade that you discussed with personnel from the district military court in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. One report was about theft committed by one of our members, and he was brought to trial and he was sentenced. He actually got a prison sentence. And then there were three more cases, again internal affairs, as it were, offences against officers of the 7th Muslim Brigade by the end of 1993. But for the most part it has nothing to do with any acts aimed at persons of another ethnicity. We were talking about abuse of power or of position, and in that respect, I remember that there were reports against three of our members.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, about this theft case that you recall. Do you recall any of the specifics about that theft? Where it occurred? What was stolen? What kind of property?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: He broke into the safe of our brigade, and it was the cashier, the treasurer of the brigade, in fact, who stole some money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And so, sir, when you told us just a few moments ago "for the most part it has nothing to do with any acts aimed at persons of another ethnicity," are you telling us that you are not aware of any member of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade being prosecuted in the district military court in Zenica for crimes against any civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that the witness was commenting on those four cases only, if my understanding is correct, the four cases mentioned by my learned friend as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of any cases that were prosecuted before the district military court in Zenica where members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were prosecuted for crimes committed against civilians or civilian property in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such cases of any members having been prosecuted for any such offences. I can say that I heard, but it was in the year 2000, that at the cantonal court there were proceedings which had been instituted against somebody from the security forces. I think his name was Isic. I can't remember his first name, really, and I can't remember what the offence is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of any cases that were prosecuted before the district military court in Travnik where members of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade were prosecuted for crimes committed against civilians or civilian property in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a single case and I never spent any time at the state Prosecution office in Travnik in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier this afternoon you were asked some questions about the security service of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and you were shown a document signed by Mr. Talic. Just so that we're clear, sir, was the Military Police Company of the 7th Muslim Brigade under the direct control of Mr. Talic, as the assistant commander for security of that brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was the assistant commander and he was in charge at the security forces. So officers and the military police were accountable to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us, sir, that Mr. Talic was also a lawyer by profession. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Earlier this afternoon my colleague from the Kubura Defence asked you some questions about -- or you responded to some questions concerning information about Mr. Asim Koricic. And at page 26, line 8, you informed us that Mr. Koricic was on official leave at the time you arrived in the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in July 1993. Do you remember saying that, sir?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: That's the information I received, that Mr. Asim Koricic was on official leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, who provided you with that information, who told you that or how you came to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember who exactly, but I asked around about who the brigade commander was. And when I was told it was Asim Koricic, I asked where he was and I was told that he was away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Did there later come a time when you were still with the brigade that Mr. Koricic returned?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Koricic, I saw him once but he was no longer with the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, were you ever aware of any investigations or disciplinary inquiries or prosecutions concerning Mr. Koricic with respect to his absence from the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. I never asked for what reason he left and who approved that. And as far as I know, there were no proceedings of any sort or perhaps I just did not get that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that Mr. Kubura was appointed the commander of the brigade in the beginning of August 1993. And my question, sir, is: During the first few weeks that you were the legal officer with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade from July 7th, 1993, until Mr. Kubura was formally appointed the commander, to whom did you report in those first few days and weeks you were with the brigade?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I was accountable to Mr. Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
