utterances.text: And during this -- these first few days and weeks, did you receive direct orders and taskings from Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Everything having to do with legal matters -- well, my instructions and orders came from Mr. Amir Kubura, and I complied with them fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And conversely, sir, you reported directly to Mr. Amir Kubura. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, from 7 July 1993 through the end of 1993, a rough approximation of how many meetings of the brigade you attended that were chaired by Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Perhaps five to six times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My objection consists of the fact the witness never mentioned the fact that Mr. Kubura was chairing any meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it has never been mentioned, Mr. Mundis. Could you rephrase your question, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you told us earlier today in response to a question from the Defence that you occasionally attended meetings of the brigade command. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, as a legal officer, but very rarely. And I said that when I became assistant commander for legal affairs, then I attended such meetings on a regular basis. But it was only as of 1994 when I received -- when I was promoted to that job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I take it, sir, that typically brigade command meetings would be chaired by the commander of the brigade, in this case Mr. Kubura. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. As of the day when he became commander, obviously he chaired these meetings or else his deputy, Mr. Halil Brzina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, prior to the time Mr. Kubura was formally appointed commander, did you attend any of the brigade command meetings in July 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. As the legal affairs officer, I was never within the command of the brigade and only occasionally, according to needs, I would have been invited to deal with one specific matter or something like that or the legal side of things that I had to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, other than these command meetings that you rarely attended, how frequently would you meet in your capacity as legal officer with Mr. Kubura during 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I rarely met Mr. Kubura, only if I had to see him because of work-related matters, if there was any need for us to meet. Yes, if I was carrying out any orders coming from him or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, your office was located in the command of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in the Bilmiste barracks in Zenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the latter half of 1993 when you were the legal officer for the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, were you ever involved personally in any combat operations or did you remain in the barracks in Bilmiste throughout those last months of 1993 or the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I did my job at the barracks. And according to needs and when I was invited, I would go out in the field together with the brigade. I did not personally participate in any combat activities. I was there as technical support. And I've mentioned this before. I was in charge with these disciplinary proceedings with regard to the members of the brigade who perpetrated these offences in the field. I did the same job that I've already described at the barracks, but in a slightly different situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when you -- tell us about these disciplinary proceedings with regard to members of the brigade. Can you elaborate a little bit on what type of offences these disciplinary proceedings covered?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I've already said this, but I can repeat it. It was either the fact that they left the brigade of their own accord or they were late coming out into the field or refusing to obey orders from their superiors or causing disturbances to the public law and order and other infringements against rules and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And these -- sir, these other infringements against rules and regulations would be categorised as minor military offences, would they not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Well, individual crimes were qualified in these rules and regulations, and then it was said, any other acts that would be harmful to the reputation of the unit. And then there was a list of priorities, as it were, telling you how serious these various infringements are, but not all of them are explained in every single detail, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you personally involved, sir, in any of these disciplinary proceedings involving crimes against the civilians or civilian property, or were all of these disciplinary proceedings involving crimes against the military or crimes against the state?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but could you repeat that question, please. I personally did not participate in what?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, let me -- let me rephrase the question. In your capacity as the legal officer or the 7th Muslim Brigade, you were -- part of your duties were conducting disciplinary proceedings. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did any of the military proceedings that you conducted or were otherwise involved in as part of your official duties involve offences committed against the civilian population or against civilian property?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No, not a single case concerned the sort of offences you have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So all of the disciplinary proceedings that were conducted during the time you were with the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade as the legal officer involved what we might call crimes against the military or crimes against the state. Would that be a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. It concerned disciplinary offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. During the time, sir, that you were the legal officer for the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, did any of the battalions of that brigade have legal officers or lawyers who were functioning in a legal capacity within those battalions?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: No. I was the only lawyer at the level of the brigade. But I have also mentioned that Mr. Nesib Talic was involved in other duties as a lawyer. In other battalions there -- the other battalions, they don't have the positions for legal officer, with the exception of the military security, who was not qualified to perform legal duties of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hasanagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is now time for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions I would like to put to you. You said that you were the only legal officer in the 7th Muslim Brigade. We know that you were a revenue inspector. As far as legal affairs are concerned, had you studied law in a way that were appropriate for you to become a lawyer? Could you tell us whether you had actually studied law.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Well, I had certain experience in the inland revenue office. This involved carrying out administrative procedures, becoming involved in disciplinary procedures, filing reports against people who owe tax. I had to compile records on tax and tax returns, too. This is the sort of work Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that I was involved in. It was possible for me to apply several laws, various laws. And I would qualify certain acts as I deemed appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that information. You said that you assumed your position in the 7th Brigade after two interviews, one with someone whom you knew, since you had played handball together. And then you mentioned the Chief of Staff, Mr. Kubura. But you said that you arrived with your family in Zenica on the 1st of January, 1993. Could you tell us, what did you do from the 1st of January, 1993, until the 7th of July. During this six-month period, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: During those six months, I immediately reported to the Territorial Defence Staff. I had to do that because I had received authorisation from the previous commander, commander Burbasic from Gorazde. He had authorised my leave. And when I arrived in Zenica, I wanted to remain a member of the army. As a result, I tried to find out how I could join up, how I could join a unit of any kind. However, given my background -- well, they had no need for someone with my background. And they also said that they didn't have a sufficient amount of weapons to engage me in some other capacity. I reported to them because all the men who were not engaged were mobilised by force; I didn't want this to happen to me. And that is why I was on the records of the Territorial Defence Staff up until the time that I was engaged. That's the only break I had in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to what we have heard from a number of witnesses, the Territorial Defence ceased to function when the ABiH, the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was established. According to all the evidence we have heard, as of January 1993 the ABiH was operational. How can you explain the fact that you remained within the Territorial Defence, given that the army was already operational? The 3rd Corps had been established. There were units present in the Zenica area; there was the 7th Muslim Brigade. Could you clarify your status. And all the more, since you know that a state of war had been declared and everyone had been mobilised. How was it possible for you to remain in a borderline situation from January to July? How is it possible for you not to become a soldier, or rather how was it possible for you to remain in this undefined situation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: I reported to the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff where records were kept on all men liable for military service. My unit of origin wasn't present in the area, and because the records were not quite correct and it was not possible for me to return to my original unit, I asked to join a unit of any kind. There were a lot of men liable for military service who had not been mobilised at the time, and this situation continued throughout the war. Men tried to avoid serving in the army, and that was never my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to a question put to you by the Defence, you said that you arrived in Zenica, if I understood this correctly, after having travelled for days and days on foot. You arrived in Zenica with your wife and two children. When you arrived in Zenica, where did you stay and how did you survive six months, since it seems that you had no resources? Where did you live and how did you feed your family for this six-month period?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Initially I lived with my wife's aunt. They helped us to start with. We stayed there for a few days, and then through friends of theirs we were able to use a small studio flat near the Zenica hospital. We lived off this aid in the beginning because a relative of my wife's aunt was one of the directors in the ironworks. He was a quite prosperous man. They provided us with food and accommodation and also I had quite a lot of friends from the Celik handball club in Zenica. And when they found out that I was in Zenica, they helped me. They provided me with food, mostly flour, and I'm very grateful to them for that. Unlike all other refugees and expelled persons, we were registered with the Red Cross and we would receive a quarter of a loaf of bread per family member every day and a little flour. This is how I lived and survived, together with my family, up until the time that I joined the 7th Brigade. And even then, I lived with 5 kilos of flour, a litre of oil, and a little cigarettes. This is something -- this is a packet I would receive once a month. And my family helped me. My wife's aunt, whose surname is Boskic [phoen], helped me then as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You have answered my question. And my last question: When you joined the 7th Brigade in July, did you hear about someone called Emir Karalic? Does the name Karalic mean anything to you.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about Emir Karalic. I never met him. I know that they called him the "brigade Emir," "the Emir of the brigade." I never knew what that meant nor did I know what sort of authority he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that you had an office that was in the vicinity of the headquarters of Mr. Kubura. And later when Mr. Kubura became the commander of the 7th Brigade, you had an office that was not far away. As far as you know, Emir Karalic, did he have an office?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Emir Karalic never had an office on the grounds of the barracks, not from the time that I arrived there. As for the situation prior to my arrival, I don't know what it was. But if he had had such an office, I think I would have been aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I give the floor to the Prosecution now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Presiding Judge asked you about your arrival in Zenica and reporting to the Territorial Defence Staff. Would it be correct to say that in 1993 in Zenica, in addition to the brigades there was the Territorial Staff, which was an integral part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And Jasmin Saric was the commander of the Municipal Staff at that time?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So when you reported to the territorial defence municipal staff you believed that you reported to one of the units that was in fact part of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that you had complied with the duties when you left Gorazde. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I thought that it was my duty to place myself at the disposal of any of the units belonging to the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in response to a question by the Presiding Judge you said that you were on the records but that there was no work for you in the Municipal Staff nor was there a sufficient amount of weapons for you to be engaged. Is that what you said? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I tried to join the 314th Brigade at the time as a lawyer; however, that position had been filled a day before I arrived by a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you have also said that there were quite a few people who were on the records but who had in fact not been engaged because weapons were lacking or there were no tasks that they could carry out at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Well, since it was impossible to have adequate regards and since there were a lot of changes in the corps, as far as the resources and men are concerned it was impossible to engage everyone on record in such a brief period of time because very often the personnel services were not sufficiently trained and they could not process all the information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I have one more question, if I have understood the situation you were in correctly. When you arrived in Zenica -- when you arrived in Zenica you -- I apologise. You were on the records but you were not under anyone's command and control, to put it in this way. You weren't engaged in a unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I wasn't engaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were waiting either for the defence secretariat to call you and to assign you to a unit or to find a unit you could join on your initiative. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, there is a question that you did not answer, a question put to you by the Presiding Judge at the beginning, and to ensure that we have all the relevant information on your educational background, could you please tell us whether you have graduated from a school of law and if so where?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN HASANAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, I graduated from the school of law in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this concludes your testimony. I would like to thank you on behalf of the Judges for having come to The Hague, as demanded by Brigadier Kubura. You have answered all the questions put to you, and I wish you a safe trip home and all the best in your professional career. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes before the break, but it seems that this pause might be transformed into an adjournment. Is there anything that the Prosecution would like to comment on? No. In that case, Defence counsel would like to tender some documents into evidence. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are quite right, Mr. President. There are two documents. One is dated the 8th of September and the other dated the 11th of September, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, the 11th of November, 1993, and the first document is the 8th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I thought that there was an implicit agreement. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No objections. Madam Registrar, could we have two numbers for these two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yeah, Your Honour, it will be DK59 and DK60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Registrar, could you tell us which document corresponds to DK59 and which one corresponds to DK60. Could we have the dates of the documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: DK59 will be dated on the 11th of November, 1993, and DK60 will be the document dated on the 8th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could I have a number, an exhibit number for the letter that was filed at the beginning of the hearing, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, Defence counsel would like an exhibit number for the letter dated the 9th of May, 2005, addressed -- sent by the general director of the agency for security and intelligence. What is your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution's view would be that it's not actually an exhibit in the sense of being evidence; it's an addendum, if you will, to the Hadzihasanovic response to the Prosecution's application to re-open. And we would -- we would have no objection to it being filed as any other pleading or annex or attachment or corrigendum to a pleading, but our position is this is not evidence and subsequently should not be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon. Stricto sensu in terms of law, this is not an exhibit from the Defence; it's in fact an annex to your response to the Prosecution's motion. But in any event this document will be annexed unless you really insist on having an DH2000 and something.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Our initial position was to file it as an annex to our response, but we would like this letter to be officially included in the file, either as an annex to our response or as an additional piece of evidence, as this is a document that could be used when presenting our arguments on Thursday. But we really don't mind, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having deliberated, the Chamber would rather consider this document to be an annex.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there anything else any of the parties would like to comment on any other issues to be raised? If not, we will see each other again on Thursday in the morning. As there is a courtroom available, the hearing will be held at 9.00 in the morning on Thursday. If that doesn't cause any problems, in that case I invite everyone to return for the hearing at 9.00 on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 19th day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.30 p.m.,
